shipped_rows.title_o: Visual biases in judging body weight

blind_target.authors: Cornelissen K. K., Bester A., Cairns P., Tovee M. J. and Cornelissen P. L.
blind_target.title: The influence of personal BMI on body size estimations ans sensitivity to body size change in anorexia spectrum disorders
blind_target.evidence_quote: In summary, the current study serves both as a replication and extension of Cornelissen et al. [17,18].
blind_target.outcome_quote: When analysing the entire clinical group, their self-estimated BMI closely matched their actual BMI, evidenced by a regression slope close to one (see Fig 2), suggesting a relatively accurate perception of own body size across the actual BMI range. However, excluding the participants with a history of bulimia nervosa and repeating the analysis, yielded results more consistent with Cornelissen et al. [17,18], as illustrated in Fig 3. Specifically, the regression slope of estimated BMI on actual BMI had a slope > 1, with accurate estimation at low actual BMI, and systematically increasing overestimation as actual BMI increased.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The authors describe agreement on the group-by-BMI interaction and psychological contribution, but a full clinical-group slope near one rather than the originals’ accelerating overestimation. Excluding bulimia participants restores the original pattern. The stated replication of the key interaction concerns one finding, not an overall verdict overriding the described difference.

luna_triage.reason: The authors state that this study retests the perceptual body-image differences in the cited original, using a revised design. The reference list identifies this candidate as reference 17. The only supplied shipped row is Cornelissen et al. (2016), “Visual biases in judging body weight,” a distinct article (reference 20), so it does not represent this original work.
luna_triage.location: Introduction (replication aim); References 17/18; supplied shipped row 1858
luna_triage.omission_quote: In summary, the current study serves both as a replication and extension of Cornelissen et al. [17,18]. We aimed to replicate the differences in perceptual body image identified in these previous studies by improving the design in the following ways: a) ensuring a more accurate alignment of actual BMI ranges across participant groups, b) incorporating measures to control for sociocultural attitudes towards appearance, and c) implementing a refined psychophysical method for body size estimation that avoided emotionally loaded language in the responses.
